summary:
Ebonyi State stands under Nigeria's national framework. The Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014 applies nationwide and reaches well beyond marriage: Human Rights Watch records that it bans cohabitation between same-sex partners, any public show of a same-sex amorous relationship, and the operation of gay clubs, societies or organisations, with prison terms of 10 to 14 years on anyone who operates, participates in or supports them. The Act also criminalises attending, organising or promoting same-sex weddings, and registering or publicly promoting gay groups.

Sexual orientation and gender identity carry criminal exposure at entry. Same-sex sexual activity has been illegal in what is now Nigeria since 1904 in the Northern Region and since 1916 across the wider territory, and secular federal law carries up to 14 years' imprisonment. Sharia law prescribes the death penalty for same-sex acts only in the states that have adopted it; Ebonyi is not among them, so the specific death-penalty exposure described for northern states does not apply on Ebonyi soil. The national prison terms do.

Enforcement against LGBTQ+ people is not confined to the statute's text. Human Rights Watch found that the Act's passage in January 2014 was immediately followed by mob attacks, arbitrary arrests, extortion and detention across the country, including the arrest without charge of 21 young men at a birthday gathering in Ibadan and repeated police detentions reported by interviewees elsewhere. The report covers Nigeria as a whole and names no Ebonyi-specific case.

Trans Nigerians face documented violence and official indifference. In August 2024 the beaten body of a 33-year-old transgender woman, a TikToker known as Abuja Area Mama, was found on a highway in Abuja hours after posting about visiting her boyfriend; police described the deceased as a man fully dressed in female clothing, and six months later no suspects had been charged. Bobrisky (Idris Okuneye), Nigeria's most prominent transgender woman, was sentenced on 12 April 2024 to six months' imprisonment without the option of a fine on naira-abuse counts and served the term in a maximum-security prison in Lagos before release on 5 August 2024; an October 2024 investigative panel found that her maximum-security placement violated the Nigerian Correctional Service Act, and contemporaneous press openly debated which section she should be held in, leaving placement between male and female wings to official discretion. Proposed bans on public cross-dressing were reported in 2022; whether any have been enacted is not settled by the sources available here.

Visitors who use dating apps face entrapment. Kito gangs lure LGBTQ+ Nigerians through Grindr and similar apps to meetings where victims are beaten, filmed and blackmailed with threats of outing. The UK foreign office's travel advisory warns LGBT+ travellers of arrest, violence, blackmail and intimidation, and that mobile networks can be suspended and curfews imposed with little notice. Nigeria offers no legal protections for LGBTQ+ people.
tangentialFactors:
Ebonyi sits in Nigeria's south-east, outside the belt of twelve northern states where Sharia-based Zina provisions add a death penalty for same-sex acts. A visitor moving north from Ebonyi crosses into materially different legal exposure, and the change is one of jurisdiction, not of atmosphere: the national prohibition statute operates in both.

The pattern described by Human Rights Watch after 2014 was country-wide rather than regional, so the absence of a named Ebonyi incident in these sources should not be read as evidence of a softer local environment. Police in Lagos were reported in March 2025 to have beaten and extorted a 24-year-old man released only after partial payment of a 50,000 naira bribe demanded for looking gay, illustrating that enforcement can function as extortion independent of any charge.

Criminalisation in Nigeria reinforced rather than replaced colonial-era codes, with the underlying offences traceable to 1904 and 1916. The 2014 Act layered organisational and expressive prohibitions on top of conduct offences, which is why public association, advocacy work and event attendance carry their own exposure alongside private conduct.
localsOnly:
Residents of Ebonyi State live under the Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014 as national law, with prison terms of 10 to 14 years for operating, participating in or supporting gay clubs, societies or organisations, and additional offences covering cohabitation, public displays of a same-sex relationship, and the registration or promotion of gay groups. Same-sex sexual activity has been an offence in Nigerian law since 1904 in the Northern Region and 1916 region-wide.

Because Ebonyi has not adopted Sharia, residents there are not exposed to the death-penalty provisions applied in the northern states; the applicable maximum is the national prison term. Nigeria provides no statutory protection on the grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity, and police have relied on the Act to justify torture and arbitrary arrests.

Placement of a transgender prisoner between male and female sections is governed by the Nigerian Correctional Service Act, which an October 2024 investigative panel found had been breached by the maximum-security assignment given to Bobrisky as a first-time offender. The panel dismissed the bribery allegations that had also been raised against prison and correctional officials.
outOfScopeNotes:
No Ebonyi State statute, directive, enforcement action or incident appears in the sources reviewed. The dossier rests entirely on the national framework and on national-level reporting; a state-specific legal instrument or case, if one exists, has not been sourced here.

Whether the proposals to criminalise public cross-dressing reported in 2022 have been enacted is unresolved in these sources, at national level or in Ebonyi. The sources also do not settle whether any Ebonyi State house of assembly has passed implementing legislation or a local anti-gay resolution of the kind adopted by some other Nigerian states.

The handling of the Abuja Area Mama killing is unresolved: the Abuja police chief ordered a thorough and discreet investigation in August 2024, and no suspects had been charged six months later. Whether any charge has followed since is not sourced.
